searches.note: Twenty eight searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's. Four were restricted to a primary body's own domain (the estate's domaine-abbatucci.com once, the INAO and the Vins de Corse wine body together once, the wine body once and the INAO once) and are read as primary through their summaries; one went to four merchants' domains for Petra Bianca; the rest to the open web for the second source of a date, a person, a blend or a method. The search on Patrimonio's decree is counted to Arena and serves Leccia; the search on Sciaccarellu and Mammolo is counted to Abbatucci and serves Leccia's question. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the bodies (the INAO for Patrimonio and Muscat du Cap Corse, the Vins de Corse listings) and the one estate with its own pages (Abbatucci), then to merchants' sheets and guides for the second source of each blend, date and method.

Where accounts disagree on a year (Canarelli's takeover, Arena's return and takeover, E Croce's founding, Abbatucci's exit from the appellations) the record gives a span or no year; where a beat rests on no source of the refuter's (the father's wishes, the first vintage of 1980, the Collection of 2006, the crates and stones of Rogliano) it is taken out.

Sources whose address names a living person (the American importer's pages, a 2021 listing of Canarelli's red under the grower's name, the island tourist board's interviews) were read in the results but never cited; the fragment's own sources were left as the author wrote them.

tested: The founding of 1968 and the son's taking over: Hameau Albert's producer history and a second producer listing give 1968, the vineyard planted then; the takeover is 1993 in iDealwine, Hameau Albert and a third listing, 1992 in Gault and Millau and Clos des Spiritueux: the year stands and the early 1990s stands.
Organic since 2002 (Ecocert) and biodynamic since 2006: Comptoir des Millésimes and Clos des Spiritueux: confirmed.

The old grapes revived (Carcaghjolu Neru, Minustellu, Genovese) and bottled apart as Vin de France (Costa Nera, Carcaghjolu Neru planted in 1997): Clos des Spiritueux, Les Passionnés du Vin: confirmed; Biancu Gentile at the estate is the library's and needs no new source.

The blend of the Figari Rouge: about 80 per cent Niellucciu in every sheet read, but the rest is Syrah 15 and Sciaccarellu 5 in the importer's sheets for 2015, 2016 and 2019 and Sciaccarellu, Carcaghjolu Neru and Syrah in Clos des Spiritueux's 2020: changed.

The making: foudres for fourteen to eighteen months in the importer's sheets and a French merchant's, destemmed with one punching down a day: the record's oak for well over a year stands, hedged as it is.
The Amphora red: fermented and raised in clay amphorae, its label Corse Figari for 2013 and 2017, Vin de France for 2022 by three merchants: changed.

Figari one of the five named zones of Vin de Corse (Calvi, Coteaux du Cap Corse, Figari, Porto-Vecchio, Sartène): the region record, with the INAO's product pages for the named zones met in the results: stands.

The questions: one key each, four options of one kind, the key not the longest; the wine question's explanation follows the new blend. The house rules: nobody living named (the grower is the son of the family), no price, no score, nothing volatile (hectares of 33 and 38 met and left out), no judging superlative, British, no dash.

tested: The return to Patrimonio: law studies in Nice and a return in 1975 by iDealwine, 1976 by the importer, so the middle of the 1970s stands; the taking of the reins is 1980 by iDealwine and 1976 by the importer, so the first vintage of 1980 cannot be settled: changed.
The father's wish for a safer life: no source of the refuter's; the importer tells instead that the father would not speak to him for a month after his return, a different story, uncited: taken out.

The decree of 13 March 1968 and Patrimonio the first appellation of Corsica: the INAO's cahier and its commission report of 2017 (the oldest Corsican appellation, first asked for in 1942) and the Vins de Corse history (Ajaccio 1971, Vin de Corse 1976): confirmed.
Organic farming: certified AB by an iDealwine listing, which adds biodynamic principles; certified organic by the importer: confirmed, and the library's biodynamic line is in tension.

Carco: one hectare of chalk, clay and limestone planted in 1987 by the importer, old Vermentino on the stony limestone of Patrimonio by Marée Haute, the father's label for the 2022: confirmed; east facing rests on IPO Wines and the author's reading of the importer.
Biancu Gentile: cuttings taken by the father and a few fellow growers from the last parcel found in the island's uplands, replanted in 1997, by IPO Wines, iDealwine and a French merchant: confirmed.

The sharing: the younger son bottling under his own name from the 2014 vintage, the Hauts de Carco white and the Carco red his; Grotte di Sole the elder son's; the father keeping the Carco white, by iDealwine, a forum and the importer: confirmed, and around 2014 stands.

tested: Faustine Rouge: Sciaccarellu 70 per cent and Niellucciu 30, about a month on the skins in concrete with daily pumping over, its own yeasts, six months in stainless steel, on the estate's own sheet: confirmed.

Vin de France: the Collection launched first as Vin de France in answer to the appellation rules, then every wine out of the appellations a few years later (iDealwine; 2013 by Vinatis, the 2011 wines already so labelled by a forum), and a Faustine of 2009 sold as Ajaccio: confirmed, no year given.
The first Cuvées Collection in 2006: no source of the refuter's, in two searches, gives the year: taken out of the story, the others note and the story question's stem.

The collection of the 1960s: the head of the estate, president of the island's chamber of agriculture, took cuttings and planted eighteen varieties on one parcel of granite sand (Vinatis, Clos des Millésimes), nineteen in iDealwine, one row of each; the first ampelographic conservatory of Corsica by Vinatis and the wine body: eighteen hedged.
The son: took the estate on in 1992 and turned it to biodynamic farming in 2000 by Hameau Albert and iDealwine, more than twenty years by the estate's own sheet: added with both years.

The Collection's names: Ministre Impérial, Général de la Révolution and Diplomate d'Empire for a general killed in 1796, his brother a diplomat and a nephew a minister of justice under the Second Empire, by the Wine Scholar Guild and the Drinks Business: forebears made historic figures of the family, since a general killed young may be no forebear in the strict sense.
Faustine named for a daughter: created at the birth of the daughter of the head of the estate, by three merchants: confirmed.
Casalabriva in the Taravo valley on granite sand: Clos des Spiritueux and the estate: confirmed. Sciaccarellu the same grape as Mammolo: the Oxford Companion and JancisRobinson.com: confirmed.

The questions: one key each, four of one kind; the story question's stem reworded without the year and its key without forebears. The house rules: nobody living named (the head of the estate and his daughter by role), no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash.

picks.ruling: kept: no swap proposed; the Corse Figari Rouge is the estate's classic red in every sheet read. The plan's note gives Sciaccarello and Nielluccio; the red is about four fifths Niellucciu, for the read-together agent.

kept: no swap proposed; Carco is the father's Patrimonio white after the sharing (Marée Haute's 2022, a forum and the importer). The plan's note puts Grotte di Sole in others, but it is the elder son's since the sharing, as the author reported, for the read-together agent.

kept: no swap proposed; Faustine is the estate's range in red, rosé and white on its own pages. The plan's why and note call Faustine an Ajaccio red; it has been Vin de France since the house left the appellations, as the author reported, for the read-together agent.
kept: no swap proposed; the Wine Scholar Guild calls the Muscatellu the house's flagship, and the plan's note asks its label name, answered Muscatellu.

kept: no swap proposed; Petra Bianca is the plan's note's own reading and a Patrimonio red of Niellucciu alone from the estate's parcel, but the estate also bottles a plain Patrimonio Rouge and a Pettale, so the record no longer calls it the red the house is known by; for the read-together agent.
